newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Moslems say they will reject poll result.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Moslems say they will reject poll result.

text.p: Bosnia's main Moslem party said on Saturday it would not recognise results from Serb-controlled territory in the country's historic post-war election.
The statement surprised international election organisers, and it was not immediately clear what repercussions it might have for post-election Bosnia.

President Alija Izetbegovic's Party of Democratic Action (SDA) charged in a letter to the U.N. Security Council that there had been serious irregularities and a lack of conditions for free and fair voting in the Bosnian Serb entity.

"The international community, in particular the sponsors of the Dayton agreement, had promised that the necessary conditions would exist at least by the date of the elections," the letter signed by SDA main board chief Halid Genjac said.

"Even before the results of the vote are known, it is clear that in many parts of Bosnia, specifically the Serb entity, the necessary conditions did not exist to provide for free and fair elections under the criteria established by Dayton or even the marginal standards of democracy," it said.

"These irregularities and the lack of the necessary conditions for free and fair elections have decisively flawed the vote. For the above reasons the SDA deems the results of the elections in the Serb entity to be legally invalid."

The letter was released to reporters as international organisers extended polling in some areas by three hours past the official 7 p.m. (1700 gmt) close, citing technical problems which had delayed voting.

The shock announcement from the SDA came only minutes after the international High Commissioner for Bosnia, Karl Bildt, had told reporters initial reports from around the country indicated the elections had gone "extremely smoothly".
"We must withhold judgment but initial reports show they took place with great dignity, great calm and great seriousness," he said.
Bildt said the manner in which the elections had been conducted bore "great testimony to the strength of the commitment to peace and to the peace process itself".
Kris Janowski, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, told reporters he had received two reports of Moslems being prevented from voting in Serb-controlled territory.
He said some 600 people living in Gorazde but voting just outside the Bosnian government town returned to their homes after waiting "hours and hours for the Serbs to open the polling station".
He said another 12 Moslems coming from the Bosnian federation town of Travnik were prevented from voting near Serb-controlled Banja Luka after Serb authorities turned their vehicle back.
Bosnian government television, controlled by the SDA party, announced on the main evening news that more time for voting had been requested at more than 100 municipalities.
Muhamed Sacirbey, Bosnian ambassador to the United Nations, told reporters in Sarajevo on Saturday night that the SDA would detail the alleged irregularities on Sunday but he added:
"The conditions (for proper elections) are not even marginally present," he said.
